newsitem.title: GERMANY: "Dike walkers" spot early signs of Oder dam leaks.
newsitem.headline: "Dike walkers" spot early signs of Oder dam leaks.

text.p: Like the proverbial Dutch boy who plugged a dike with his finger, the "dike walkers" on the river Oder have a lonely job, but without them there would be little chance of holding back the mighty river.

Day and night local villagers have been going out onto the dikes, carrying yellow flags and walkie-talkies, looking for signs of seepage as the river presses relentlessly against the weakening wall that holds back the Oder in eastern Germany.

"If I see water seeping through, then I put this flag in the ground and call in the location on my walkie-talkie," said Rudi Goellnitz, a farmer in Bleyen, who is just one of hundreds of walkers who have joined the fight to save the Oder dikes.

More than 10,000 soldiers and thousands more aid workers, water rescue teams and volunteer fire fighters have been struggling for almost two weeks in an increasingly desperate effort to plug each new leak in the dike, hoping to prevent a break.

Some locals can well remember the last time the dam broke. That was in 1947, near Reitwein, and the water flowed unabated through a crack in the wall filling the Oderbruch valley, a fertile basin some 17 km (11 miles) wide and 50 km (36 miles) long.

That the dam has held this long is a miracle, officials say. Although the rain has stopped, the water is only slowly receding and it still has over one and a half metres (five feet) to fall before the dike walkers can feel confident.

Martin Nabaum, 58, was sitting on in a garden chair on the edge of the dike near the village of Neuruednitz, patting his dog Fester and smoking a cigarette as he eyed a stick in the water that showed the level at just under seven metres.
"Fester's nervous," he said, rubbing the German shepherd behind its ears. "He can feel that something's wrong and he just won't stay home."
Scratching his unshaven chin, Nabaum said he had been sitting at the dike, watching the metre stick for 40 hours.
"It's risen two cm since 6 a.m.," he said, adding that he did not mind staying all night on the dike. "If the dam breaks I'll lose all my possesions. Why should I stay home?"

Udo Eckner, 33, passed Nabaum as he made his rounds on the dike. While soldiers and aid workers battled day and night to reinforce the dike, Eckner hung his head, tired and almost out of hope, describing how at dozens of points along the dike water was seeping through the foundations.
"It's as if you were to wring out a washcloth," he said.
"When the water comes through brownish carrying bits and pieces of earth then we know it's serious and we have to fill the spot immediately with sandbags."

In some places the water laps up against the top of the dike. In others it appears harmless and only locals can point some distance out into a spot in the rushing water where the shore used to be as bits of turf and trees float by.
Further away, at the inland base of the dam, large pools have built up in places where the river seeps through.
Walking there is dangerous because the seepage has turned the farmer's field to swamp and large underground pools have formed that could swallow a person whole in seconds.
"The worst part of it all," said Eckner, "is that people are getting complacent. In the beginning everyone was upset, but you get used to a catastrophe after a while. Man is a creature of habit."

Goellnitz appeared to agree. Bearded and donning a blue seaman's cap typical for the region, he said: "Sure, I've taken some precautions, but I've lived here for 30 years. The dam will hold. It's not as bad as they're saying on TV."
